title: Quickstart
text: Quickstart From nothing to a build you can follow in the browser, in five steps. Every step also works in the terminal UI; the two share one build service.

title: 1. Install
text: Download the version you want from GitHub Releases (replace 1.2.3): sudo apt install ./bitloom_1.2.3_all.deb # Debian / Ubuntu: dependencies included On other distributions and WSL2, install the source archive in a virtual environment: tar -xzf bitloom-1.2.3.tar.gz && cd bitloom-1.2.3 python3 -m venv ~/.bitloom-venv && ~/.bitloom-venv/bin/pip install . Check the result with bitloom --version. Real builds also need what your project uses: kas or kas-container with Docker or Podman, or an initialised Poky checkout. See installation for checksums and the release SBOM.

title: 2. Look around on the samples
text: bitloom --web --demo Bitloom prints the dashboard URL, which carries its access token, and opens your browser. The demo has a Scarthgap and a Wrynose sample workspace: switch between them with the profile menu. Press ? for the keys, Ctrl+K for the palette, 1 to 8 for the sections. Nothing here runs a real build.

title: 3. Connect your project
text: Start Bitloom from your project folder: cd ~/src/my-product bitloom --web With no profile yet, the dashboard opens Configuration → Set up a project on that folder and proposes how it builds, with the evidence it found: Your project has Bitloom proposes kas files (kas/*.yml) a kas-container profile per configuration, with a work directory on a Linux filesystem a launcher script that runs kas, used as YML=kas/board.yml ./run_kas.sh build a wrapper profile per product; BitBake commands run as ./run_kas.sh shell -c '…', and the build folder comes from the script's KAS_WORK_DIR a Poky or OE-Core checkout a host profile that sources oe-init-build-env Animation Guided setup on a launcher project with two products Pick a proposal, check the fields (each is explained and checked as you type) and press Save. When one launcher builds several products, Save all products creates one profile each. Details: Projects and guided setup.

title: 4. Build and follow
text: In Builds (1), click the target field or press t: it lists the image recipes found in your layers, the kas target and the images already built first. Any recipe works too. Press b (or Build). The job appears at the top of the history, with live output, progress and an ETA. When it ends, Summary (u) groups errors, warnings and failed tasks; Compare (d) shows what changed since the previous run. A failed build's summary starts with a diagnosis of the real cause: the failed task, its log, the lines that matter and the next step. Operations (q) queues any of the 79 operations: one recipe's compile, a clean, a dry run, an SDK, an SBOM or CVE check. Operations your Yocto release does not have are not offered, and say what to use instead. Image (4) opens what you built: every file with its size and the package and recipe that installs it, and Change it with an append for anything you want different. See Image explorer. Animation A real force compile of busybox followed live, then its summary Close the browser whenever you like: the build service keeps the queue and the history, and bitloom --web reconnects. Optional notifications tell you when a build ends (Daily helpers).

title: 5. The same, in the terminal
text: bitloom Opens the terminal UI on the same service, profiles and history: useful over SSH. Numbers open sections, letters act, / searches, ? lists every key, P switches profile. See the keyboard reference.

title: Where next
text: Web dashboard: every section, notifications, the API. SBOM, CRA and releases: SBOM quality, vulnerabilities and their exports, CRA readiness. Studio: your own layer, distribution, machine, image or recipe, explained field by field. User guide: profiles and runtimes, caches, analysis, troubleshooting. Teams and CI/CD: headless --ci runs, team profiles, launcher scripts in depth.

title: Install from a GitHub release
text: Open the GitHub Releases page and download the assets for the version you want. Replace 1.2.3 below with that version.

title: Debian / Ubuntu
text: Download bitloom_1.2.3_all.deb, then install it from the download directory: sudo apt install ./bitloom_1.2.3_all.deb bitloom --demo Requires Python 3.10+ on Debian/Ubuntu. Python application dependencies are included under /opt/bitloom/lib; no pip installation is needed. Docker, Podman, kas and Yocto remain separate tools for real builds. Remove Bitloom with sudo apt remove bitloom.

title: Other Linux distributions / WSL2
text: Download bitloom-1.2.3.tar.gz and install in a virtual environment: tar -xzf bitloom-1.2.3.tar.gz cd bitloom-1.2.3 python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install . .venv/bin/bitloom --demo Alternatively, install the release wheel with .venv/bin/python -m pip install /path/to/bitloom-1.2.3-py3-none-any.whl. Source and wheel installation require Python 3.10+, venv support and internet access to install dependencies. WSL users should install inside their Linux distribution.

title: Verify downloaded assets
text: Download SHA256SUMS alongside the packages, then run sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS in the same directory. Check that the package you downloaded reports OK. bitloom --version prints the installed version. Every release also carries bitloom-1.2.3.spdx.json, an SPDX 2.3 SBOM of what the packages contain: Bitloom and each bundled Python package (Textual, Rich and their dependencies) with its version, SPDX licence identifier and package URL. The Debian package installs the same file as /usr/share/doc/bitloom/sbom.spdx.json, for the software inventory of the machines you install it on.

title: How releases are made
text: Releases are cut with Actions → Release Bitloom → Run workflow and a version such as 1.2.3. The workflow refuses versions that already have a tag, and stable releases from any branch other than main (tick pre-release to publish from another branch). It runs the test suite, builds the source archive, wheel, Debian package, SBOM and SHA256SUMS, installs the .deb on a clean runner and checks bitloom --version, the bundled SBOM and a smoke run, keeps the assets with the workflow run, then commits the version into pyproject.toml and bitloom/__init__.py on a release commit, tags it v1.2.3 and publishes the GitHub release from that tag with generated notes. The release commit is reachable only from its tag: main keeps the development version. Build the same assets locally with python tools/build_release.py 1.2.3 --output dist/release (needs build, wheel and dpkg-deb).

title: Fresh checkout demo
text: Run ./setup-demo.sh from the cloned checkout to create or reuse .venv, install dependencies and launch the sample TUI. Requires Bash, Python 3.10+ with venv support on Linux or WSL2, and internet access for installation. No Docker, kas or Yocto installation is needed for the sample data. Use ./setup-demo.sh --no-launch to prepare without launching, then .venv/bin/bitloom --demo to start later. --dev installs test dependencies; --python python3.12 or PYTHON selects the interpreter for a new environment. The script also works when invoked from another directory. All demo data stays under .bitloom in the checkout. The demo has three profiles; press P to switch: Profile Workspace Shows demo .bitloom/demo Generic sample: recipes, a failing task log, a console build, caches demo-scarthgap .bitloom/demo-scarthgap Poky layout detected as 5.0 LTS, SPDX 2.2 SBOM, cve-check summary; Wrynose-only operations are explained and refused demo-wrynose .bitloom/demo-wrynose Split OE-Core layout detected as 6.0 LTS, SPDX 3 SBOM with VEX, sbom-cve-check report Every sample file is labelled; the demo never simulates a successful Yocto build. The terminal adapts while resizing: below 105 columns or 30 rows it hides the navigator and side panes; below 30 rows it also hides the overview. Below 75 columns or 22 rows it hides history and metrics to preserve output. Resize to restore panels. F8/F9 switches sections and F2/F4/F7 opens commands/profiles/themes even when toolbar controls are hidden. Verifi

title: Profiles and paths
text: Profiles are local JSON stored at .bitloom/profiles.json by default. State is stored at .bitloom/; both paths can be set on the command line. The file is atomically replaced with mode 0600. Profile names must be unique; queued jobs retain a copy of the original profile. Field Meaning name Unique profile identifier root Absolute or relative project root (resolved on the host) build_dir Build directory, relative to root or absolute on host mode host, kas, container, kas-container or wrapper (a project launcher script, see Teams) init_script Host/container init script; autodetects oe-init-build-env or poky/oe-init-build-env kas_file kas configuration path(s), including colon-separated composition engine Docker or Podman for generic container mode image Builder image for a fresh container container_name Existing container name; empty starts a fresh temporary container container_root Project mount path inside a generic container; default /work machine, distro Environment overrides passed through BitBake's allow-list downloads, sstate Host paths used by cache inventory; these do not modify BitBake configuration environment String environment variables; kas variables control kas paths/runtime container_args Array of additional Docker/Podman arguments targets Suggested targets; the first fills the toolbar source_mappings Absolute runtime-to-host directory mappings for Developer IDE exports launcher, launcher_shell wrapper mode: the script argv and how it runs a command ({command}) A

title: Host
text: Set root to your checkout. The TUI sources the init script in bash and executes a quoted argument list. You can also start from an already initialized shell and leave init_script empty. Target fields accept one or more BitBake targets separated by spaces (core-image-minimal busybox, virtual/kernel, mc:qemuarm:core-image-minimal); anything else, such as shell operators, is refused before queueing. Task and variable fields are checked the same way.

title: kas
text: Set mode to kas and point kas_file to your YAML. BitBake/devtool commands execute with kas shell FILE -c COMMAND; kas actions call the appropriate subcommand directly. Install kas in your preferred environment.

title: kas-container
text: Install the official kas-container wrapper and a functioning Docker or Podman runtime. Set KAS_CONTAINER_ENGINE, KAS_WORK_DIR and optionally KAS_BUILD_DIR in environment. Use a dedicated work directory distinct from the Git source repository. The wrapper supplies containerized kas and Yocto dependencies. kas-container does not forward every arbitrary host environment variable into its container. Put Yocto overrides in kas YAML or use officially supported kas environment variables. The machine/distro profile fields map to KAS_MACHINE/KAS_DISTRO in kas modes; you can also set these directly. Set container engine through KAS_CONTAINER_ENGINE, not the generic engine field.

title: Generic Docker / Podman
text: Set mode to container, engine and image. New containers bind root at container_root, use the current UID/GID and have a unique name. The image must contain bash and your build dependencies. BitBake should be the final exec process for graceful signalling. Existing container_name uses exec instead; that container must already mount the project at container_root. build_dir must be inside root. External caches require explicit mounts plus matching paths in your build configuration. Runtime args must be JSON strings, such as ["--network", "host"]; review privileged options yourself.

title: Build and development workflows
text: Enter one target or recipe in the toolbar and press Build or F2. Filter the command list by group/name. Required inputs appear dynamically. Review the exact invocation and queue it. Builds and utilities share a serial queue to avoid two servers modifying one build directory. The Build pane persists operation, profile, status, timestamps, exit code and log path. Enter on a row loads its log. Retry uses original command and profile even if you have switched profiles. Live progress comes from standard Running task N of M messages. History timestamps are stored in UTC. Use recipe browsing to locate metadata, open files, build or start devtool modify. The metadata browser indexes local files, including inactive layers; Show layers, Show recipes, Show appends and Show overlaid recipes ask BitBake for evaluated state. Kernel and bootloader configuration: Kernel menuconfig (any recipe with a Kconfig, such as virtual/kernel or busybox), Export kernel config changes (diffconfig, a fragment for your append) and Save kernel defconfig work on the kernel; U-Boot menuconfig and Export U-Boot config changes do the same for the machine's bootloader (virtual/bootloader). Keep the changes as .cfg fragments in an append in your layer, never in the work folder. Machines without a bootloader recipe (qemux86-64) refuse the U-Boot actions before running. Interactive actions suspend Textual and give the real terminal to devshell, menuconfig, QEMU or kas shell. They require a real terminal and cannot

title: Terminal layout
text: Bitloom is fully usable without a mouse; the keyboard reference lists every key and ? shows it inside the TUI. The top bar shows the profile, runtime, MACHINE, DISTRO, the detected Yocto release, the service connection and the clock; the brand shimmers while the service is building. The numbered navigator lists sections 1–0; [/] or F8/F9 cycle through them and the section's list receives focus. Each section has single-letter actions, shown in the footer and in front of every button label (for example s stop, r retry, e errors only in Builds). Letters typed into a field never trigger them; / or Ctrl+W focuses the section filter and Esc returns to the list. Editors use nano keys: ^O write, ^X exit (asks before discarding changes), ^W search, ^K/^U cut and uncut lines, ^G help. Status cards show the current job with a spinner, task and setscene counts, CPU/RAM with a CPU sparkline, and disk usage; the Build card flashes green or red when a job ends. The progress bar is indeterminate until BitBake reports task counts. P switches profile, t edits the build target (several targets separated by spaces; Enter builds them; ↓ lists the image recipes found in the project, → accepts the inline suggestion), b builds, Ctrl+P lists sections, actions and all operations. Screenshot Keyboard reference overlay 140 × 42 shows the complete workspace. Below 105 columns or 30 rows, tabs replace the navigator and side panes disappear; short terminals also hide the task monitor and overview. Below 75

title: Know when a build ends
text: Configuration → o (or the Build notifications panel in the web Configuration section) chooses how the build service announces finished jobs: outcomes (success, failed, cancelled) and a minimum duration, so short commands stay quiet; a desktop notification: notify-send on Linux, a Windows notification when Bitloom runs in WSL; a webhook: an ntfy topic (phone push, with high priority for failures), a Slack, Teams or Mattermost incoming webhook ({"text": …}), or JSON with every job detail for your own tooling. The service sends them, so they arrive even when no TUI or browser is open; an open TUI also rings the terminal bell. ^T sends a test. Settings live in <state>/notifications.json (mode 0600, as webhook URLs may be secret). In the web dashboard the bell button in the top bar additionally enables browser notifications for builds that end while the tab is in the background. Screenshot Notification settings

title: How long is left
text: While a build runs, the Tasks card and the web progress line show an ETA. It combines the current task rate (after enough tasks to be meaningful) with the median duration of the last successful runs of the same command in the same profile, and says which it used.

title: What changed since the last run
text: Builds → d (web: the Compare tab) compares the selected job with the previous run of the same command: duration, tasks executed against setscene tasks restored from sstate, sstate hit rate, reused tasks, warnings that are new or gone, and new errors. Numbers inside messages are normalised so the same warning with another version is not reported as new. Many more executed tasks with fewer setscene tasks point at changed metadata or a cold cache; Analysis → Why rebuilding? explains the signatures. Screenshot Comparison with the previous run

title: What fills tmp/work
text: Caches → w (web Configuration: tmp/work usage, CLI: bitloom --work-usage) measures each recipe's work directory (bounded to 30 seconds on huge trees), lists the largest, says whether rm_work is enabled and gives bitbake -c clean commands for the biggest. INHERIT += "rm_work" removes work directories after each recipe builds; keep recipes you debug with RM_WORK_EXCLUDE.

title: Errors and log search
text: Failures generate a notification and refresh the task-log browser. Analysis → Failure diagnosis anchors on the root cause instead of the first line mentioning a failure: compiler errors, the first make *** line with the output leading to it, out-of-memory kills, full disks, fetch and patch failures and pseudo aborts. It lists the failed tasks and maps known causes to a next step, for example retrying a MakeMaker "Makefile has been rebuilt" race, pinning the peeled commit of an annotated kas tag, or bitbake -c clean <recipe> when a build interrupted by a restart left empty object files behind (undefined references to main). These rules come from failures seen on real Scarthgap and Wrynose builds. Builds → c opens console builds that were started outside Bitloom (details). Select a failed build in history and use Failed task log in Task logs to read paths explicitly reported by BitBake through the original runtime. This works with container-only paths too; at most ten logs are queued per click. Search selected logs case-insensitively with three surrounding lines, or toggle errors-only. Pause freezes live display while output continues to be written to disk; Resume reloads the captured tail. The live view keeps 5,000 lines; searches inspect the complete file and cap the rendered result. Export copies the original complete log to .bitloom/exports. Task logs are discovered under the standard tmp/work/ARCH/RECIPE/VERSION/temp hierarchy and ordered by modification time. Custom TMPDI

title: Workbench
text: Environment: Resolve env for the chosen target, wait for success, then Load. Filter both variable names and values. Capturing two environments for the same target/profile enables Env diff. Literal exported values are compared; function bodies and assignment provenance remain in the original log. Dependencies: Generate graph for a target and wait for success. Choose Dependencies and Load to read task-depends.dot from the configured host-visible build directory. If the build directory is container-only, Load queues a read through the original runtime and parses its persisted output. Filter nodes to explore task relationships. The first 20,000 edges are indexed. Enter an exact node name in the filter and choose Why this task? to traverse required and reverse dependencies. Traversal detects cycles and limits each direction to 200 nodes. Build history: Enable buildhistory and BUILDHISTORY_COMMIT in local.conf, build an image, then open Build history diff. The report shows recent Git commits and changes between the newest two commits. Signatures: Use Dump signatures, Explain sstate differences, Read signature file or Compare signature files. Signature commands use BitBake tools from the selected release rather than decoding undocumented binary formats.

title: Root filesystem inspection
text: Select a tar rootfs archive in Artifacts and use Rootfs inventory. The report lists file type, mode, numeric UID/GID, size and link targets. Archives are never extracted and links are never followed. The inventory is bounded to 20,000 entries. Other image formats require their own tooling.

title: Analysis reports
text: Open Analysis in the navigator or tab bar, choose a report, and press Analyze. Export saves the displayed report under the state directory's exports folder. Search metadata: enter a literal phrase. Search is case-insensitive and covers indexed recipes, appends, classes, kas YAML and layer.conf, including inactive layers. Results contain paths and line numbers. Files above 2 MB or unreadable files are skipped; output stops at 1,000 matches. Container-only metadata must be made host-visible to be indexed. Compare manifests: enter before and after image manifest paths. Standard package architecture version rows and two-column package version rows are supported. Added/removed packages and changed versions are listed separately; architecture is part of identity. Conflicting versions and malformed rows are rejected. Each manifest is limited to 100,000 lines. Paths refer to host-visible files, including copied container artifacts. Sstate efficiency: leave the first path blank to use the selected build log, or enter another log path. The report reads actual Sstate summary counts and computes hit rate for wanted tasks and coverage including current tasks. A zero denominator or missing count is shown as unavailable. This does not establish which cache objects are safe to remove. Warning groups: select or enter a build log. Identical messages are counted after removing the timestamp/logger prefix; the 200 most frequent groups are shown. Different recipe paths and message text remain dis

title: Cache and download maintenance
text: Scan either Downloads or Shared state to view names, size, age and relative paths. Inventory is capped at 20,000 files. The scan total is the indexed total, not necessarily the entire cache. Set an age of at least one day and open Prune plan. It lists concrete files and estimated bytes; nothing is removed before Execute plan. Pruning excludes symlinks, .lock/.done markers, Git checkout internals and files whose sibling lock exists. Each file's path, size, modification time and sibling lock are checked again at deletion. Only files inside the selected root can be deleted. The TUI refuses a plan while its own jobs are active/queued. Other machines/builders cannot be detected. Age is not proof that an artifact is unused. Keep shared caches and offline source requirements in mind. Recipe clean keeps downloads/sstate; cleansstate removes local recipe shared state; cleanall also deletes recipe downloads. Remote sstate mirrors are unaffected by local inventory pruning. Download audit reports possible partial files, lock files and orphan completion markers. For actual source integrity checking, use the recipe fetch task and its SRC_URI checksums.

title: Releases and compatibility
text: Versions reports local repository branches, commit IDs, Git descriptions, dirty status and literal LAYERSERIES_COMPAT declarations against locally detected LAYERSERIES_CORENAMES. Dynamic expressions can require manual review. Metadata parse is authoritative. Use one profile/build directory per release. The TUI does not switch active Git branches underneath a running build, silently migrate local.conf syntax or mix caches without your configuration.

title: Configuration editing
text: local.conf, bblayers.conf and metadata are editable. Save creates a timestamped backup, refuses to overwrite a file changed externally, and atomically replaces the contents. Files above 2 MB and binary files are not opened in the editor. Close without saving discards in-editor changes. Review changes with your usual Git tooling. Example snippets cover buildhistory/buildstats, mirrors, shared caches, offline builds, mirror tarballs, thread limits and optional image/security classes.

title: Troubleshooting
text: bitbake not found: configure an init script or launch from a sourced environment. kas or kas-container not found: the build service keeps the PATH of the shell that started it, plus the bin directory of Bitloom's own Python environment. Install kas in that environment or on the system PATH, then restart the service when idle (bitloom --service-stop). bitloom: …profiles.json is not valid JSON (or another profiles error): the message names the file and the problem. Fix it, or move it away: the next start opens the guided setup. An empty file counts as a first start; without "active" the first profile is used. history.sqlite3 cannot be used: the build history database is damaged (for example after a disk full). Move it away to start a new history; logs under <state>/logs remain. security-reviews.json reported as damaged: CRA readiness and Vulnerabilities show the problem instead of the reviews, and recording a review is refused, so the file is never overwritten. Fix the JSON (an object of package/CVE entries) or move it away. do_sbom_cve_check cannot find …rootfs-<timestamp>.spdx.json: a stale image SBOM; see SBOM, CRA and releases. Docker permission denied: the user running Bitloom must have permission to the Docker socket; the app never changes daemon permissions. Docker Snap and /tmp: Snap's daemon can see a different /tmp from the host. A bind mount may be created as root in the daemon namespace. Prefer a dedicated Linux directory visible to both namespaces, or initialize on

title: Practical limits
text: Each command remains subject to the selected Yocto release, runtime, device access and configuration. Inventory scans are bounded, age-based pruning does not perform signature reachability analysis, and no cache is pruned automatically. External builders sharing a cache cannot be detected reliably. Logs and profiles can contain proprietary paths or credentials; review exports before sharing them. Custom commands accept argv, not shell expressions. Unit and UI tests in CI do not run a Yocto build; the container integration builds are separate, opt-in validations (see validation).

title: Documentation and verification
text: pip install -e '.[dev]' python -m pytest -q # unit and UI tests, no Yocto build needed pip install pillow cairosvg playwright # optional capture tooling python tools/capture_docs.py # TUI screenshots and GIFs python tools/capture_web.py # web dashboard (Playwright with Chromium) python tools/generate_reference.py # commands.md and keyboard.md from the code python tools/serve_docs.py --port 8000 # rebuild the HTML and serve docs/ python tools/check_docs.py # links, anchors and page behaviour The Pages workflow publishes docs/ on pushes to main when the repository has Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions (private repositories need a plan that includes Pages); otherwise the run is skipped with a notice. python tools/capture_docs.py captures the real Textual interface with Pilot and exports SVG/PNG/GIF. It uses labelled demo data. python tools/validate_kas.py executes a real image build through Runner and records a JSON result. Read validation.md for evidence from the current development session.

title: Persistent build service and reconnecting
text: Real launches now use an independent local build service by default. Closing the TUI, pressing Ctrl+Q, or losing the terminal detaches the client: queued and running jobs remain owned by the service. Reopen Bitloom with the same --state directory to reconnect. Jobs retain their original profile, commands and complete logs. Multiple clients can observe the same service. bitloom --config .bitloom/profiles.json --state .bitloom bitloom --state .bitloom --service-status bitloom --state .bitloom --service-stop # idle service only bitloom --embedded # exit stops owned jobs Demo mode remains embedded. F5 still explicitly interrupts a selected job through the service. The service refuses an idle-stop request when jobs remain queued/running; use F5 first if interruption is intended. A Unix socket in a private Linux /tmp/bitloom-services-UID directory works even when the project lives on a WSL Windows mount. Connections are restricted to the same UID. History remains under the selected state directory. This is local persistence, not reboot recovery or a distributed scheduler: a crashed service marks incomplete history interrupted on its next start and does not automatically replay work.

title: Runtime filesystem and artifacts
text: The Analysis selector now provides Runtime directory, Runtime file, Edit runtime file and Export runtime artifact. Enter an absolute path as seen by the selected runtime, such as /work/build/conf/local.conf in kas-container. These operations run Python inside that runtime through the same command routing as builds. Python 3 must exist there. Directory previews stop at 2,000 entries; text previews/edits at 2 MiB. Runtime editing opens an actual editor, rejects files changed since the preview, refuses symlink edits, preserves the original file in a content-addressed backup and replaces the file atomically. Saving is blocked while this client's build queue is active. External programs remain responsible for their own edits. Binary export streams a file up to 1 GiB into a temporary local file and verifies both SHA-256 and byte count before committing it. The second path is the local destination; leaving it blank uses the state's exports directory. Existing destinations are never overwritten. This handles artifacts visible only inside the container, including a Docker Snap daemon's private filesystem. It does not require mounting or extracting an image.

title: Evidence workflows
text: Analysis choice Input and result Why rebuilding? Enter one recipe; queue release-native bitbake -S printdiff and evaluated environment. Analyze again after completion to link the stored explanation, the two newest available sigdata files per task/work variant, release-native signature comparisons and referenced variable values. The chosen signature timestamps must match your intended before/after states. Use F2 to capture a fresh printdiff; a matching cache can legitimately report no difference. Failure diagnosis Select a build log or enter a runtime task log path. Classify fetch/patch/compile/QA/rootfs evidence and show the first diagnostic with context and reported task-log paths. Suggestions are troubleshooting steps, not automatic fixes. Package provenance Set the top target field to an image recipe and enter a package or absolute installed file path. Evaluate the image, read runtime pkgdata, map files to packages/recipes and show a shortest path from PACKAGE_INSTALL/IMAGE_INSTALL through runtime dependencies. Build preflight Enter a runtime build directory or leave blank. Check writable parent, disk headroom, free inodes and configuration presence in the actual filesystem. BLOCK and WARN are distinct; this advisory report does not intercept queued commands. Devtool review Enter the runtime source Git directory. Review status, uncommitted diff, commits and patch text before using build/deploy/finish/reset from F2. It does not calculate the release-specific final patch tra

title: Coordinating shared caches
text: Bitloom builders take a shared .bitloom-coordination.lock on host-visible download and sstate directories. Maintenance takes an exclusive lock, so cooperating services cannot prune while another Bitloom builder uses the cache. A separate build-directory lease prevents duplicate builders across local state directories. Existing .lock and .done protection also applies when executing a plan directly. These are advisory locks. External BitBake processes, container-only cache paths and builders that do not take the same lock are not coordinated. Signature reference plans are conservative: one build's stamps are not an exhaustive record of every cache user. For release-specific removal, coordinate all builders and use that release's scripts/sstate-cache-management.sh after inspecting its own help/options. Bitloom does not infer reachability from age or silently invoke a destructive cache script.

title: Terminal themes
text: Press F7 or the toolbar's Themes button. Choose a palette to preview it immediately, then Save theme to persist it or Cancel/Escape to restore the palette you opened with. Changes affect terminal backgrounds, surfaces, tables, selection colors, modal dialogs and semantic status colors. Source previews use a matching light/dark syntax palette on their next refresh. title: Build, launch and try the local Yocto workspace
text: Run these commands from the repository root in a Linux/WSL terminal. Bitloom is a Python application: editable installation is sufficient for development; no native compilation is required.

title: Install for development
text: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -e '.[dev]' bitloom --help bitloom --demo If themes appear monochrome and your shell sets NO_COLOR, run unset NO_COLOR before launching. In this prepared workspace, .venv and kas-container already exist. You can start directly with source .venv/bin/activate.

title: Build distributable packages
text: source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install 'setuptools>=61' build wheel python -m build --no-isolation Outputs are dist/bitloom-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl and dist/bitloom-0.1.0.tar.gz. The distribution and executable are both named bitloom. The source archive includes the English manuals, Pages assets, examples and integration tools. To install the wheel into another environment: python3 -m venv /tmp/bitloom-wheel /tmp/bitloom-wheel/bin/python -m pip install dist/bitloom-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl /tmp/bitloom-wheel/bin/bitloom --help

title: Open the already built local test workspace
text: The verified local workspace uses Poky yocto-5.0.8 / Scarthgap, qemux86-64, core-image-minimal and a pinned kas container image. Yocto tools execute inside Docker; the host runs only the TUI and container wrapper. .validation is local generated state and is intentionally absent from a fresh Git clone. source .venv/bin/activate python tools/prepare_validation.py bitloom --config .validation/profiles.json --state .validation A recorded result is historical evidence: temporary work mounts can be removed. Check /work/build through the runtime before relying on it; if absent, prepare a new workspace with python tools/validate_developer.py --build and launch .developer-validation/profiles.json as explained in the testbook. The helper recreates the test profile from .validation/result.json when available. It preserves history and other profiles, uses the recorded workspace and does not build anything. The actual work directory is recorded in .validation/result.json; with Docker Snap, its contents are in the daemon's namespace and may appear empty on the host. In the container, the build directory is /work/build. Use Analysis runtime tools to browse it. Keep core-image-minimal in the top target field and press Build for an incremental image build. Existing matching task outputs are reused. Select its history row to follow the complete log. F2 opens recipe tasks, fetch, SDK, layers and devtool actions; change the target to busybox to inspect or build one recipe. In Analysis, choose Bu

title: Reproduce on a fresh machine
text: Docker must be available and the build work directory must be on a Linux filesystem. Install the official wrapper if needed: source .venv/bin/activate curl -fL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siemens/kas/4.8.1/kas-container -o .venv/bin/kas-container chmod +x .venv/bin/kas-container python tools/prepare_validation.py --work /tmp/bitloom-kas-validation --engine docker bitloom --config .validation/profiles.json --state .validation Press Build to initialize and build the image. The first build downloads repositories/sources and needs substantially more time and disk than the verified incremental run. The helper does not repair container mount permissions: if Docker Snap creates the dedicated mount as root, follow the runtime troubleshooting guide. For scripted verification, with the service stopped: python tools/validate_kas.py --work /tmp/bitloom-kas-validation --engine docker python tools/prepare_validation.py python tools/probe_kas.py python tools/probe_workflows.py validate_kas.py builds the image and verifies its rootfs; probes then exercise real runtime operations. probe_workflows.py submits a warm build to a separate persistent service and stops that service after completion. Unit/UI checks run with python -m pytest -q; they do not require a Yocto build.

title: Preview the Pages site locally
text: python -m pip install '.[docs]' python tools/serve_docs.py --port 8000 # rebuilds the HTML, then serves docs/ python tools/serve_docs.py --port 9000 --no-build --open --host changes the bind address (loopback by default). Screenshots in the HTML pages are collapsed and load only when expanded.

title: Gentle colors and focus
text: F7 offers Soft Slate, a muted dark gray palette, and Linen, a warm light palette. Focusing report or log panes highlights the border without tinting the entire background. If a true-color terminal such as Windows Terminal renders saturated blue blocks, check TERM and COLORTERM and try COLORTERM=truecolor bitloom with your usual profile arguments. Limited-color terminals still use their available colors.

title: Navigation and elapsed time
text: F8 selects the previous workspace section; F9 selects the next, including Developer, Analysis and Help. F10 opens Developer directly. These keys work with conventional terminal escape sequences. Alt+number bindings remain available on terminals sending compatible key events, but are not the recommended navigation keys. Running history rows update their elapsed time once per second, independently of log output; finished durations remain fixed.

title: Hands-on kas: layers and recipes
text: Start the verified workspace with python tools/prepare_validation.py, then bitloom --config .validation/profiles.json --state .validation. Docker must be running. Use F2 to open commands and F8/F9 to change sections. First build busybox, repeat the build, run Clean recipe, and build again. Compare executed and reused tasks. Clean recipe + sstate removes the recipe's local shared state too; mirrors can still supply cached results. Build core-image-minimal afterward to inspect image assembly.

title: Create a layer and a small recipe
text: From F2, open Open kas shell. The following commands run inside the container, with the BitBake environment initialized. /work/meta-bitloom persists in this profile's dedicated work mount. bitbake-layers create-layer /work/meta-bitloom mkdir -p /work/meta-bitloom/recipes-example/bitloom-hello cat > /work/meta-bitloom/recipes-example/bitloom-hello/bitloom-hello_1.0.bb <<'EOF' SUMMARY = "Bitloom learning example" LICENSE = "CLOSED" S = "${WORKDIR}" do_install() { install -d ${D}${bindir} printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "Hello from Bitloom v1"\n' > ${D}${bindir}/bitloom-hello chmod 0755 ${D}${bindir}/bitloom-hello } EOF exit CLOSED is used for this private exercise to avoid needing a separate license file; use the actual license and checksum for distributable recipes. Layer creation and registration are separate operations. F2 also provides Create layer and Add layer, but a layer registered only in bblayers.conf may be lost when kas regenerates configuration.

title: Register the layer reproducibly
text: Create kas-experiment.yml at the root of the Bitloom checkout, using your host editor: header: version: 14 includes: - tests/integration/kas-minimal.yml repos: experiment: path: /work/meta-bitloom local_conf_header: bitloom-experiment: | IMAGE_INSTALL:append = " bitloom-hello" This absolute layer path intentionally targets the container workspace above. In F4 duplicate the kas integration profile, retaining its container environment and KAS_WORK_DIR, and set kas_file to kas-experiment.yml. Run kas build to apply the configuration. The local layer is declared in kas rather than only in a generated configuration file. Do not commit kas-experiment.yml until you decide whether this container-specific configuration belongs in your project. Build target bitloom-hello, then build core-image-minimal and inspect its package manifest for bitloom-hello. To edit the recipe, use the Analysis runtime file reader/editor on /work/meta-bitloom/recipes-example/bitloom-hello/bitloom-hello_1.0.bb, or open the kas shell and use an available editor. Change the greeting to v2 and rebuild the recipe and image. BitBake should detect the metadata change; a clean is usually unnecessary.

title: Extend an existing recipe
text: Keep upstream recipes intact and add a matching .bbappend in your layer. For example, create recipes-core/busybox/busybox_%.bbappend containing: SUMMARY:append = " (Bitloom experiment)" Evaluate BusyBox's environment and inspect SUMMARY to verify the append. For source development use Modify recipe (devtool modify), edit the extracted source directory reported by devtool, then Devtool build. Commit source changes before Devtool finish into /work/meta-bitloom; that exports the recipe changes/patches to your layer. Devtool reset removes workspace integration when you want to return to the layer recipe. Source files may remain, so inspect them before removing anything. References: Yocto layers, kas configuration.

title: Create files and refresh external changes
text: Metadata's New file button and Analysis's Create runtime file operation open an editor with an absolute destination path and templates for empty text, private example recipes and .bbappend files. Select the template before entering your content. Create file creates missing parent folders and atomically publishes the file without overwriting existing files or symlinks. Builds queued or running in this session must finish before metadata creation or editing. With kas/container profiles use runtime paths, for example /work/meta-bitloom/recipes-example/hello/hello_1.0.bb. The directory is shown in Analysis after creation. Local metadata remains a host filesystem index; container-only files are viewed through runtime directory/file operations. Host metadata additions, edits and deletions are detected every five seconds and refresh the index when changed. Open runtime directory listings refresh every fifteen seconds while idle, with a 2,000-entry limit. Dialogs pause automatic scans. F3 rescans local metadata; Analyze refreshes the current runtime directory immediately. To follow the hands-on tutorial entirely through Bitloom: use F2 Create layer for /work/meta-bitloom, then New file to create the .bb recipe and any .bbappend files. Create the kas experiment YAML in the host checkout using your editor, since a container profile's file dialog targets the container filesystem. Register the layer in kas as described above. Existing container files can be edited through Analysis → Edit

title: Connected Developer workflows
text: F10 opens the Developer workbench. Its guide documents all sixteen views, field meanings, queued operations, stale-file detection, immutable captures and baseline comparison. New layer previews complete CMake/Meson/Make/Python/Rust fixtures and registers them through a new kas composition or bitbake-layers. Clone, also in F4, preserves the original profile and selects a separate build directory. Optional source_mappings maps absolute runtime roots to real host-visible directories for IDE exports. New owned kas-container jobs have unique Docker/Podman names and labels. Force stop records the exact container's stop result before recipe recovery is offered. Graceful draining remains disabled for kas wrappers; native kas and external containers retain unconfirmed-server guards. Shutdown evidence displays the original job observations separately from a fresh probe namespace. After upgrading, let an existing persistent service finish its queue and stop that idle service once; the next launch loads the new code. Existing history is retained. The Developer acceptance cases give concrete experiments for every workflow, including optional hardware, kernel and SDK prerequisites.

title: Projects and guided setup
text: Projects and guided setup Bitloom works with many projects at once: every project is a profile, and switching project is switching profile (P). The Projects hub opens existing folders, creates new Yocto projects and clones projects from GitHub or any Git server. The guided setup reads how a folder builds and proposes a ready-to-use profile. Open the hub with Configuration → w, Ctrl+P → Projects, or the Projects panel in the web dashboard's Configuration section (8). Screenshot Projects hub with recent projects

title: Open an existing project: guided setup
text: In the hub press o, type the project folder and press Enter (or use Set up a project in the web Configuration section). Bitloom scans the folder (two levels deep, read-only) and proposes profiles, each with the evidence it found: Launcher scripts: executable scripts that call kas/kas-container, for example a project's run_build.sh. Each product configuration becomes its own wrapper proposal, titled the way you run it (YML=kas/board-a.yml ./run_build.sh build): the variable the script reads (such as YML) is set to that file, and machine and targets come from it, following includes. Files that other kas files include, or that name no machine, are fragments and are not offered as products. The build folder is read from the script's KAS_WORK_DIR (defaults such as ${KAS_WORK_DIR:-$HOME/build}, $PWD, the script's own folder, helper variables like TOP=$(cd $(dirname $0) && pwd) and per-product forms like build-${YML%.yml} or $(basename $YML .yml) are expanded); when the script computes it at run time, set KAS_WORK_DIR in the profile. kas configurations: YAML files with a kas header; MACHINE and target are read from the file. kas-container is proposed when available (or when kas is missing), with a separate work directory under ~/bitloom-work. bitbake-setup workspaces (the official setup tool of recent BitBake): a setup folder (build/init-build-env, config/, layers/) or the top folder holding several (bitbake-builds/ with site.conf). Each becomes a host profile that sources build/ini

title: Project launcher scripts
text: When the folder has a script that runs kas, the proposal uses the wrapper runtime: kas operations call ./script <subcommand> and BitBake commands call ./script shell -c '<command>', with the environment variables from the profile (for example YML=boards/board.yml). For BitBake commands and runtime probes the script must forward shell -c and keep standard input open. See Teams, CI/CD and setup for the details and a minimal example script.

title: Create a new project
text: Press n in the hub (web: New project). A few choices give a buildable project: Field Meaning Project name Lowercase; also the profile name Folder A new or empty folder (defaults to ~/yocto/<name>) Yocto release Scarthgap 5.0 LTS (Poky repository) or Wrynose 6.0 LTS (bitbake, openembedded-core and meta-yocto) MACHINE, DISTRO, image Start on QEMU with poky; derive your board and distribution later with Studio Runtime kas-container (recommended) or kas on the host Product layer Creates meta-<name> registered in the kas file Bitloom writes kas.yml pinned to the release tags verified by its own real builds (yocto-5.0.8 and yocto-6.0.2, with the commits the tags point to), a README, a .gitignore, the optional layer, and runs git init. The profile becomes active; the first build downloads layers and sources. Update the pinned tags deliberately, and use Generate kas lock file to record exact revisions. Screenshot New project form with the generated kas.yml

title: Clone from GitHub or Git
text: Press g in the hub (web: Clone from Git), enter an https://, ssh://, git@ or file:// URL, the destination (suggested from the URL until you edit it) and an optional branch or tag. Your Git credentials and SSH agent are used as in a terminal. The clone runs as a normal job, so you follow its progress in Builds. When it succeeds, the guided setup opens on the new folder.

title: Recent projects
text: The hub lists recently opened, created, cloned and set-up folders (stored in <state>/projects.json) together with every profile root. Enter switches to the folder's profile, or runs the guided setup if the folder is not set up yet.

title: Web dashboard
text: The Configuration section has the same three parts: Projects (recent list, New project with live file preview, Clone from Git), Set up a project (scan, proposals, form, live checks, Save and use), and the health checks. Saving or creating selects the new profile in the header at once; a finished clone raises a toast with Set it up. Screenshot Projects in the web dashboard

title: API
text: Method and path Purpose GET /api/projects Recent projects, releases, machines and images POST /api/projects/preview, /create Plan or create a new project {name, dir, release, machine, distro, target, runtime, layer, owner} POST /api/projects/clone Clone {url, dest, branch} as a job; returns the job id GET /api/setup/scan?dir=… Proposals for a folder POST /api/setup/check, /save Check or save {profile}; saving makes it active

title: Web dashboard
text: Web dashboard bitloom --web serves a browser dashboard for the same build service the TUI uses. Builds queued from the browser and from the terminal share one serial queue and one history, so you can start a build in the TUI, follow it on a laptop or phone, and retry it from either place. Screenshot Web dashboard following a running build

title: Start it
text: bitloom --web # loopback only, opens a browser bitloom --web --no-browser --port 9000 # pick the port; 0 chooses a free one bitloom --web --config .bitloom/profiles.json --state .bitloom The command prints a URL such as http://127.0.0.1:8765/#token=… and opens it in a graphical browser: on WSL the Windows browser (through wslview when installed, otherwise PowerShell). Text-mode browsers such as lynx or w3m are never started, because they would take over the terminal; without a graphical browser Bitloom only prints the URL. --no-browser skips opening. The token lives in the URL fragment: it is never sent in requests, the page keeps it for the browser tab and sends it as an X-Bitloom-Token header. Ctrl+C stops the web server only; builds keep running in the service. --state must match the TUI to see the same history. The dashboard needs only the Python standard library. It is not a multi-user server: anyone holding the URL can queue builds for your profiles.

title: Remote access
text: Keep the default loopback address and tunnel it: ssh -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 build-server --host 0.0.0.0 listens on every interface and prints a warning; use it only on a trusted network. On loopback the server also checks the Host header, which defeats DNS-rebinding attacks.

title: Sections
text: Key Section What it shows 1 Builds History with live spinners, the selected job with an animated progress bar (stripes while running, indeterminate until BitBake reports task counts), streaming output, search with context, errors-only filter, stop, graceful stop and retry. Console builds started outside Bitloom appear under the history. 2 Recipes Every layer on the left with its file count (example and selftest layers last); on the right the folders of the selected layer (recipes-core, classes-recipe…) open on click, with recipe name, version, kind and path. Filter by kind (Recipes, Images, Appends, Classes, kas) and search as you type; Use as target puts a recipe in the build field. 3 Task logs tmp/work/*/temp/log.* files with search and an errors-only view. Only indexed task logs can be read. 4 Image The built root filesystem, folder by folder, with sizes, owners and the package and recipe behind every file; Services: what starts on the device (systemd units or SysV scripts in boot order, udev rules, D-Bus); Device tree: the deployed DTBs decompiled, with enabled and disabled devices; the biggest packages and folders; Which recipe installs… for any file or package, with Change it with an append. See Image explorer. 5 SBOM & CRA Release support, SBOM quality gauges, VEX status, vulnerabilities from cve-check, sbom-cve-check and Grype, CRA readiness checks, the regulation timeline and every SBOM option with its explanation. See SBOM, CRA and releases. 6 Studio Create a produc

title: Build target
text: The target field in the top bar is a combobox. Click it, press t or ↓ to list the image recipes found in the project's layers: the kas target: and images already built come first, example and test images last, each with its layer and SUMMARY. Type to filter, ↑/↓ to choose, Enter to pick, Enter again to build. Any other recipe or several space-separated targets can still be typed. An image recipe is a .bb that inherits core-image or image, or requires another image recipe. Only files with "image" in their path are read, so the list is ready in a few milliseconds. Animation Typing in the target field filters the image recipes; Enter picks one Animation A real force compile of busybox followed live, then its summary (about three times faster) The build detail has Toaster-style tabs computed from the stored log: Summary (errors, warnings, failed tasks), Sstate reuse, grouped Warnings, observed task Timings and Compare with the previous run of the same command. A running build shows its ETA next to the task count. Screenshot Build summary tab The progress line above the tabs shows the task count, the percentage and the ETA; a dot marks where BitBake is, and a failed build keeps a ✖ where it stopped. When a build fails, a toast offers its summary, which starts with the failure diagnosis: the category, the failed tasks, their logs, the lines that caused it and the next step. Animation A failed sample build: the toast, then the summary opening on the diagnosis

title: Notifications and animations
text: The bell button in the top bar turns on browser notifications for builds that end while the tab is in the background; the build service's own desktop and webhook notifications are configured in Configuration (see Daily helpers). New jobs slide in at the top of the history; existing rows update in place, so the list never flickers while a job runs. Toasts slide in for every state change of a job: started, succeeded, failed (with a button that opens the summary) and cancelled. Hover a toast to pause its countdown; failures stay longer. Cards count up, rings and meters animate, the CPU card draws a live sparkline, and views fade in. With the operating system's reduce motion setting, all animations are disabled.

title: Image explorer
text: Image explorer What did the build actually put on the device, where does each file come from, and how do you change it? The Image explorer answers from what BitBake left on disk after the build: no BitBake run, no device needed. Open it with section 4 of the web dashboard, Ctrl+K → Explore the built image, or ask Which recipe installs… from anywhere (web, TUI, command line). Screenshot The Image explorer on a real Wrynose core-image-minimal

title: What you see
text: The image of the active profile: every image built for every machine, newest first. Bitloom reads the root filesystem archive in tmp/deploy/images/<machine> (tar.bz2, tar.gz, tar.xz, or tar.zst when zstd is installed), or the rootfs folder in tmp/work while it still exists (without rm_work). Add a tar type to IMAGE_FSTYPES if your image only produces disk images. Totals: the size on the device, the number of files and of packages. Biggest packages and biggest folders: where the space goes. Click a package to see which recipe builds it; click a folder to open it. The file tree, folder by folder, each entry with its size, a bar relative to the folder, and the package · recipe that installs it. Symbolic links show their target. The selected file: size, permissions, owner and group, the package and recipe, the layer (yours or upstream), the images that contain it and what pulls it in (the packages that depend on it, such as packagegroup-core-boot), the existing .bbappend files of that recipe, and the content when it is a small text file.

title: What starts on the device
text: Services (next to Files) shows what the image runs and what reacts to it, read from the root filesystem, each entry with the package and recipe that installs it: the init system (systemd, SysV init or BusyBox init) and, with systemd, the default target; systemd units: the ones that start at boot (enabled by a link in /etc/systemd/system/*.wants, with the target that wants them), the ones installed but not enabled (started on demand by a socket, D-Bus or another unit, or not at all) and the masked ones (linked to /dev/null), with their description and ExecStart; SysV init scripts in start order: rcS.d first, then the runlevel, with their S number; the scripts run only at shutdown and reboot, and the helpers linked nowhere, are listed apart; udev rules in the order udev applies them, with the number of rules and their first comment; a file in /etc/udev/rules.d replaces the one with the same name in /lib, and a link to /dev/null disables it; D-Bus: services started on request (their bus name and systemd unit) and bus policies. Select an entry to open its file with the usual details: owner, package, recipe, layer and Change it with an append. To change what starts, append to the recipe (SYSTEMD_AUTO_ENABLE, SYSTEMD_SERVICE, INITSCRIPT_PARAMS) or take its package out of the image. Screenshot Services of a real Wrynose core-image-minimal: init scripts in boot order, the selected script and its recipe The same list is in the TUI (Analysis → Services in the image) and on the command

title: Device tree
text: Device tree lists the .dtb and .dtbo files the build deployed in tmp/deploy/images/<machine> (the short names, not the versioned copies; the machine of the selected image first) and opens one decompiled, with no dtc needed: Bitloom reads the flattened device tree itself, and the DTS text matches what dtc -I dtb -O dts gives (verified by compiling it back with the build's own dtc). The board: model, compatible strings, boot arguments, the console (stdout-path), memory. Enabled devices and disabled devices (status = "disabled"), each with its path and first compatible string: select one to jump to its node. The DTS text with search: type, Enter for the next match, Shift+Enter for the previous one. Phandles are shown as &label where the meaning is clear (interrupt-parent = <&interrupt_controller_8000>). An overlay (.dtbo) is marked as such: the bootloader applies it on top of a base tree. To change a device tree, add a .dts or .dtsi to your BSP layer and list it in KERNEL_DEVICETREE, or ship an overlay; never edit the kernel's own tree. x86 and most QEMU machines deploy no device tree; the demo workspace has a labelled sample board.
