title: Change it
text: Under the file, Bitloom says what to do: the recipe comes from an upstream layer (Poky, OE-Core, meta-yocto…): never edit it there. Change it with an append opens Studio on a Recipe append already filled in: the recipe, its folder (recipes-core…) and, for a file in /etc, the file itself, starting from its current content on the device. Edit it with edit before creating, review, create, rebuild; your layer already appends that recipe: change your append; the recipe is in your layer: edit the recipe. Some files are in no package: /etc/passwd, /etc/group, /etc/shadow, /etc/ld.so.cache… They are made while the image is assembled, by useradd, ldconfig, package post-install scripts or the image recipe's ROOTFS_POSTPROCESS_COMMAND. Bitloom says so and points to where to change them (for example EXTRA_USERS_PARAMS in the image recipe for users). Animation From the image to the append that changes /etc/motd

title: Which recipe installs…?
text: Type a file on the device (/etc/motd), a package as installed (libc6) or a recipe (glibc) in the Image view's search, the Ctrl+K palette, the TUI's Analysis → Which recipe installs…, or on the command line: $ bitloom --who-installs /etc/inittab WHICH RECIPE INSTALLS: /etc/inittab sysvinit-inittab (sysvinit-inittab) ships this file recipe sysvinit-inittab 2.88dsf …/meta/recipes-core/sysvinit/sysvinit-inittab_2.88dsf.bb layer meta (upstream) file /etc/inittab image core-image-minimal (qemux86-64) pulled in by sysvinit change add recipes-core/sysvinit-inittab/sysvinit-inittab_%.bbappend to your layer (Studio → Recipe append) It is the same information as oe-pkgdata-util find-path and lookup-recipe, plus the layer, the images, the dependants and the advice, read from tmp/pkgdata/<machine>/runtime and the image manifests. Package renames are followed (libc6 is the glibc package). A file name without a path (inittab) also works. It answers for what has been packaged: build the recipe or the image once first.

title: Practical limits
text: Ownership comes from package data (FILES_INFO); files created at image assembly time have no package, as explained above. Disk images (ext4, wic) are not opened: Bitloom needs a tar archive or the rootfs folder. Very large images take a few seconds the first time (the archive is read once, then cached until it changes). Owners come from the archive. The rootfs folder in tmp/work belongs to your build user (pseudo keeps the real owners in its own database), so owners are not shown for it. The TUI offers Which recipe installs… and Services in the image in Analysis and the rootfs inventory in Artifacts (i); the folder-by-folder explorer is in the web dashboard.

title: SBOM, CRA and Yocto releases
text: SBOM, CRA and Yocto releases Bitloom reads the evidence your build already produces and tells you, release by release, what is missing for a machine-readable SBOM and for vulnerability handling under the EU Cyber Resilience Act. It reports engineering evidence; it is not a conformity assessment or legal advice.

title: Release awareness
text: Bitloom detects the Yocto series from LAYERSERIES_CORENAMES in the core layer (Poky, separate OE-Core or kas workspaces) and shows it in the top bar, the web header and the CRA report. Series Version Support SBOM and CVE tooling kirkstone 4.0 LTS until 2026-04 SPDX 2.2 (create-spdx), cve-check scarthgap 5.0 LTS until 2028-04 SPDX 2.2 by default, cve-check styhead … whinlatter 5.1 – 5.3 7 months each SPDX 3.0 default, cve-check wrynose 6.0 LTS until 2030-04 SPDX 3.0 only, VEX in recipe SBOMs, sbom-cve-check replaces cve-check Every operation, SBOM option, CRA check and Studio default asks one registry of release capabilities (bitloom/capabilities.py, listed in the command reference). Each capability is decided by evidence in the project first: the class in its layers (vex.bbclass, sbom-cve-check.bbclass, create-spdx-3.0.bbclass…), the tool in its own BitBake (bitbake-config-build, bitbake-setup), the kind of workspace; the release number is the fallback when the layers are not visible from Bitloom. A backport is therefore offered, and a class a release lacks is not. Configuration shows the answer for the active project (web: What this release can do; TUI: the Release · health rows). When a feature does not exist in the project's release, Bitloom says so and offers what the release can do: the command center marks the operation (not in this release), disables queueing and names the alternative (for example cve-check on Scarthgap instead of sbom-cve-check); the web dashboard ref

title: SBOM quality
text: Artifacts → s (or bitloom --sbom) analyses the newest image and SDK SBOMs offline: SPDX 3.0 JSON-LD (IMAGE.spdx.json, Styhead and later). SPDX 2.2 images, which ship IMAGE.spdx.tar.zst: Bitloom joins the image manifest with the per-package and recipe documents in tmp/deploy/spdx, so no zstd tooling is needed. An SPDX 3 image SBOM from OpenEmbedded also describes the recipes that produced the image (including -native build tools), the downloaded source archives and the image itself. Coverage is measured on the installed packages (software_primaryPurpose install), the components that ship; the report lists how many other elements the document describes. For each SBOM it reports the share of packages with a version, a PURL, a CPE, licence information and a supplier, the VEX status counts (affected, under investigation, fixed, not affected) with the affected CVE identifiers, the CVEs that SPDX 2.2 recipes record as fixed, and the packages without a licence or identifier. The Organization: OpenEmbedded () placeholder does not count as a supplier: set your company in the SBOM settings. Screenshot SBOM quality of the Wrynose sample workspace

title: CRA readiness
text: Configuration → c (or bitloom --cra, exit code 2 when a check warns) lists: Check Evidence Yocto release support Release series, LTS and community support end Machine-readable SBOM Newest image SBOM and its format Component identifiers, licences PURL/CPE and licence coverage (90% threshold) Vulnerability status (VEX) VEX assessments in the newest SBOM Vulnerability analysis sbom-cve-check / VEX reports or the cve-check summary Change traceability buildhistory in INHERIT Vulnerability dispositions Reviews recorded in Developer → Security, with owner and expiry Reproducibility evidence Reproducibility bundles exported from Analysis It also shows the CRA timeline: reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents (Article 14) apply from 11 September 2026; the essential requirements of Annex I apply from 11 December 2027. Screenshot CRA readiness for the Wrynose sample

title: EN 40000
text: The CRA harmonised standards are being written by CEN/CENELEC JTC 13 as the EN 40000 series. prEN 40000-1-3 covers vulnerability handling: receipt, assessment, remediation, communication and tracking of vulnerabilities, corresponding to Annex I Part II of the regulation. It is a draft at the time of writing. Bitloom does not implement or certify the standard. Its compliance features are organised around the evidence such a process needs from the build: a per-build SBOM whose identifiers allow matching, VEX status and CVE analysis per release, dispositions with an owner and an expiry date, change traceability through buildhistory, and reproducibility bundles.

title: Vulnerabilities
text: SBOM-based CVE tools cross the components of an SBOM with vulnerability databases. Artifacts → v (web: the Vulnerabilities panel in SBOM & CRA, CLI: bitloom --vulns) merges their results into one list, one row per CVE and package, the most urgent first: Source File Release sbom-cve-check (Bootlin) tmp/deploy/images/<machine>/<image>.rootfs.sbom-cve-check.yocto.json Wrynose, enabled with the core/yocto/sbom-cve-check fragment cve-check tmp/log/cve/cve-summary.json, <image>.rootfs.json up to Whinlatter (INHERIT += "cve-check") Grype (Anchore) <state>/vulnerability-scans/*.grype.json any release with an SPDX JSON SBOM Each finding shows the severity (from CVSS v4, then v3, then v2), the score, the CVE with its link, the package and version, the status (Unpatched, Patched, Ignored) with the tool's detail (for example version-in-range or not-applicable-config), and the review recorded in Bitloom. Filter by source, status (unpatched, all, reviewed), minimum CVSS and text (/). r records a review for the selected CVE: owner, reason or evidence reference, and an expiry date (the same dispositions as Developer → Security). A review never marks the upstream vulnerability as fixed. g scans the newest SPDX JSON SBOM with Grype (when installed) as a visible job; the list reopens with the results when it finishes. SPDX 2.2 images ship their SBOM as an archive: extract it first. x exports the findings shown (same filters) to <state>/exports in the format you choose; the web dashboard has the

title: Export formats
text: Format Use Markdown (.md) A readable report for a ticket, a wiki or a pull request: summary by severity and status, the unpatched findings with NVD, CVE.org and OSV links, a section per package, the patched and ignored list in a collapsible block, and the Yocto remediation steps. HTML (.html) The same report as a self-contained page in light or dark theme; print it to PDF to share it. CSV (.csv) Spreadsheets; every row carries its NVD and OSV links. JSON (.json) Scripts and dashboards: sources, filters, counts and every finding with its links. SARIF 2.1.0 (.sarif) GitHub code scanning and other SARIF viewers: one alert per unpatched finding, ranked by CVSS (security-severity), with remediation help. From the command line or CI: bitloom --vulns --format md -o vulnerabilities.md # unpatched findings bitloom --vulns --format html --all-statuses -o report.html # with patched and ignored bitloom --vulns --format sarif -o bitloom.sarif --min-cvss 7 # then upload with github/codeql-action/upload-sarif Identifiers link to NVD, CVE.org and OSV for CVEs and to the GitHub advisory database for GHSA identifiers; the tool's own reference link is kept as well. VulnScout (Savoir-faire Linux) reads the same SPDX SBOMs, cve-check JSON, Yocto VEX and Grype results and adds a web assessment workflow and a CI mode (--match-condition, exit code 2); its meta-vulnscout layer runs it from BitBake. CRA readiness lists Unpatched vulnerabilities (critical and high count as a warning), and CI can gate o

title: SBOM settings
text: Configuration → s manages SBOM, vulnerability and traceability options. Each option explains what it does, why it matters for the CRA and which releases provide it. Options whose first release is not confirmed are marked ?; press v to verify the variable in your runtime with bitbake-getvar. Option Writes Generate SPDX SBOMs INHERIT += "create-spdx" Package / image supplier (SPDX 3) SPDX_PACKAGE_SUPPLIER_name/_type, SPDX_IMAGE_SUPPLIER_name/_type Supplier (SPDX 2.2) SPDX_SUPPLIER = "Organization: …" VEX data in SBOMs `SPDX_INCLUDE_VEX = none VEX metadata class INHERIT += "vex" sbom-cve-check (Wrynose) bitbake-config-build enable-fragment core/yocto/sbom-cve-check Warn on unpatched CVEs SBOM_CVE_CHECK_SHOW_WARNINGS = "1" cve-check (before Wrynose) INHERIT += "cve-check" Source files, compiled sources, kernel config, PACKAGECONFIG, readable JSON SPDX_INCLUDE_SOURCES, SPDX_INCLUDE_COMPILED_SOURCES, SPDX_INCLUDE_KERNEL_CONFIG, SPDX_INCLUDE_PACKAGECONFIG, SPDX_PRETTY Build history INHERIT += "buildhistory", BUILDHISTORY_COMMIT = "1" Enter/Space toggles or edits, ^O applies. Host and container profiles get one managed block in conf/local.conf (with a timestamped backup); kas profiles get a bitloom-sbom.yml overlay appended to the profile's kas_file, because kas regenerates local.conf. Fragments are enabled or disabled by queueing bitbake-config-build. Screenshot SBOM settings with explanations and release windows

title: New operations
text: Operation Command Release Recipe CVE analysis from its SBOM bitbake -c sbom_cve_check_recipe RECIPE wrynose+ Create recipe SBOM bitbake -c create_recipe_sbom RECIPE wrynose+ Generate VEX metadata bitbake -c generate_vex RECIPE probed Enable / disable sbom-cve-check bitbake-config-build enable-fragment / disable-fragment core/yocto/sbom-cve-check wrynose+ Run recipe CVE check bitbake -c cve_check RECIPE until whinlatter

title: Try it
text: bitloom --demo creates demo-scarthgap and demo-wrynose next to the generic demo. Press P to switch: the Wrynose sample has an SPDX 3 SBOM with VEX and an sbom-cve-check report; the Scarthgap sample has an SPDX 2.2 SBOM and a cve-check summary. Every sample file is labelled; nothing claims a real build. Sources: Yocto security manual: checking for vulnerabilities, VulnScout, Yocto Project 6.0 release notes, Yocto reference manual: classes and variables, Bootlin: sbom-cve-check in Wrynose, EN 40000-1-3 overview.

title: Studio
text: Studio Studio creates the metadata of your own product: a product layer, your distribution instead of Poky, machines, images, recipes and appends. Defaults follow the detected Yocto release, and you see every file, and everything Create will do, before anything is written. Open it with Recipes → c in the TUI, Ctrl+P → Studio, or section 6 of the web dashboard. Screenshot Studio creating a distribution on Wrynose

title: The web Studio: one step at a time
text: In the web dashboard (section 6) Studio is a guided path, not an editor: What do you want to create? Six cards: product layer, distribution, machine, image, application recipe, recipe append. Each says what you get (for example recipes-core/images/acme-image.bb) and what it is for. The steps follow the form's sections: Where the files go, Name and identity, What goes in, Policies. One step is shown at a time; Next (or Enter in a text field) and Back move between them, and the step list on the left marks steps done (✓) or with a problem (!). Any step can be reopened from the list. Where it goes (right): the layer and only the folders the new files go into, with the files already there for context and the new ones marked new; below, the content of every file Create will write, highlighted. Focusing a field highlights the lines it writes. To change the generated text yourself, switch on edit before creating; the tab is then marked as edited and Create writes your version. Review and create: your choices, exactly what Create will do (files, kas overlay or bitbake-layers add-layer, profile changes) and any problem to fix. Create (or Ctrl+Enter) writes the files; nothing is written before. What next: the actions that make sense now: build the new image or recipe, make it the build target, rebuild the recipe an append changes, add a distribution or an image to a new layer, see the files in Recipes, or create something else. Existing files are never modified or overwritten, and upstr

title: How the form reads
text: The form is split into numbered sections: Where the files go, Name and identity, What goes in and Policies. Each field has a plain label; the BitBake variable it sets is shown next to it (for example Product name · DISTRO_NAME), so the form is readable without knowing Yocto and still tells experts exactly what is written. Choices explain themselves. Under a drop-down, a line says what the selected option means (systemd: full service manager; default from Wrynose). Feature chips show their meaning on hover or focus, and the line under them lists what is selected. Help that quotes an example follows what you type (You build it with: bitbake gateway-image). The preview follows the field. Focusing a field highlights the lines it writes and switches to the file that contains them. Errors point at the field, mark its step with ! and are listed in the review; Create stays disabled until they are fixed. No layer of your own yet? The Layer field says so: a new layer (default meta-acme) is created together with the files, shown as new layer in Where it goes. The layer choice is kept when you switch between kinds. In the TUI (Recipes → c) the same form and plan appear in one dialog: kinds on the left, the form in the middle, the steps and the files on the right.

title: What you can create
text: Kind Files Notes Product layer conf/layer.conf, README.md, COPYING.MIT Collection, priority, LAYERDEPENDS, LAYERSERIES_COMPAT from the detected release Distribution conf/distro/<id>.conf Based on Poky (require conf/distro/poky.conf) or standalone OE-Core defaults; DISTRO_NAME/VERSION, MAINTAINER, vendors, INIT_MANAGER, DISTRO_FEATURES to add and remove, package format, security_flags.inc, SBOM policy with the supplier Machine conf/machine/<id>.conf Derived from a reference machine (require + MACHINEOVERRIDES), MACHINE_FEATURES, SERIAL_CONSOLES, preferred kernel Image recipes-core/images/<name>.bb inherit core-image or extend an existing image, IMAGE_FEATURES, packages, IMAGE_FSTYPES, extra space Application recipe recipes-example/<name>/… Licensed sample with CMake, Meson, Make, Python or Rust sources Recipe append recipes-*/<recipe>/<recipe>_%.bbappend FILESEXTRAPATHS, an installed file, extra assignments Release-dependent choices are applied for you: INIT_MANAGER defaults to systemd on Wrynose, which made it the default. The image developer-access features follow 5.1: debug-tweaks was split into allow-empty-password, empty-root-password and allow-root-login; Studio refuses debug-tweaks on 5.1 and later. Appends read files from UNPACKDIR on 5.1 and later, WORKDIR before. The SBOM supplier uses SPDX_PACKAGE_SUPPLIER/SPDX_IMAGE_SUPPLIER on SPDX 3 releases and SPDX_SUPPLIER on SPDX 2.2 releases.

title: Where files go
text: Choose an existing product layer (upstream layers such as meta, meta-poky and fetched repositories are never offered) or new layer…. Studio writes only inside the project root or KAS_WORK_DIR, refuses any file that already exists and writes all files or none.

title: Registration
text: Profile After creation host, container A new layer is registered with a queued bitbake-layers add-layer. For a distribution or machine, Use for this profile sets the profile's DISTRO/MACHINE. kas, kas-container Studio writes kas-studio-<layer>.yml (the new layer as a repository plus distro:, machine: or target:) and appends it to the profile's kas_file. Team profiles are not modified: clone them first. wrapper The overlay is written; add it to the configuration your launcher passes to kas. Images and recipes set the build target, so b builds them next.

title: Keyboard
text: ↑/↓ choose the kind, Tab moves through the fields (the preview follows), Space toggles list entries, ^O creates, Esc closes. In the web dashboard the kinds are cards, chips toggle with Enter/Space, and file tabs switch the preview.

title: Best practices
text: Best practices Does your project follow the way the Yocto Project recommends to work? Practices reviews your layers and build configuration against the advice of the Yocto documentation, shows what you already follow, what needs attention (with the file and line) and how to fix it. Your team decides which rules apply, how serious each one is, and can add its own. Open it with section 7 of the web dashboard or Ctrl+K → Best practices. In CI, run bitloom --practices (see below). Screenshot Practices on a real Wrynose project: the score, what needs attention, every rule

title: What is checked
text: Only your layers are judged: the ones of your product, not Poky, OE-Core, meta-openembedded or other upstream layers. Upstream layers are only checked for local changes (they should have none). Each rule links to the page of the Yocto documentation it comes from. Area Rules Layers named meta-<name>; layer.conf declares collection, pattern, priority and LAYERSERIES_COMPAT; the compatible series includes the release you build; LAYERDEPENDS names layers the project has; a README, a SECURITY.md and a licence in each layer; layer.conf sets only layer variables; BSP, distribution and software in separate layers; layers under Git Upstream Poky, OE-Core and the other upstream checkouts are not modified Appends upstream recipes are extended with a .bbappend, not copied; every append has its recipe; FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/files:"; the colon override syntax (:append, not _append); product images are your own recipes, not appends to core-image-* Recipes name_version.bb in lowercase; LICENSE and LIC_FILES_CHKSUM; sha256sum for downloads; Git sources pinned with SRCREV (no AUTOREV); patches with Upstream-Status Security no development access in the product (debug-tweaks, allow-empty-password, allow-root-login, empty-root-password) Configuration DL_DIR and SSTATE_DIR shared outside the build directory; a distribution of your own instead of poky; product settings in layers rather than local.conf; buildhistory; rm_work Each rule is an error, a warning or a suggestion. The scor

title: Tune it for your project
text: Every rule has a switch and a severity: switch a rule off when it does not apply (a project that deliberately ships poky, a BSP-only repository). It moves to Switched off and no longer counts; change its severity: make rm-work an error on the shared build server, or layer-security-policy a suggestion for an internal layer. The choices are saved in bitloom-practices.json at the project root. Commit it: everyone who opens the project, and CI, applies the same rules.

title: Company rules
text: Add a company rule opens a short wizard. Nothing to learn first: every field has a ? that explains it, examples you can click, and a sentence at the top that says the rule in plain words as you build it (An error unless DISTRO is exactly acme in your configuration). What to check. Start from an example (every recipe names a maintainer, every recipe has a SUMMARY, no internal host names, each layer has CODEOWNERS, products build our distribution, a distro feature is required) or pick one of the four kinds of check. Details. The files and the text to look for, the file each layer must have, or the variable and its value. Try it on this project runs the check at once, without saving: your project follows it, or the places that do not, with file and line. Name and explain. A title (the id is made from it), how serious it is (an error fails CI), and one sentence each for why it matters and how to fix it: they are shown to whoever breaks the rule. Screenshot Step 1: start from an example or choose the kind of check Screenshot Step 2: an example filled in, the help of a field open, and Try it on the project The four kinds of check: Check Passes when Example files-must-match every file matching files in your layers contains pattern (a regular expression, line by line) every recipe sets MAINTAINER files-must-not-match no file matching files contains pattern no x11 in configuration files, no internal host names layer-file-exists each of your layers has the file or folder at path a CODE

title: Export and CI
text: Export downloads the review as Markdown (for a merge request or a wiki), JSON (for tools) or text.

title: In CI
text: $ bitloom --practices Yocto best practices · 81% followed 0 errors · 1 warning · 4 suggestions · your layers: meta-acme APPENDS ✔ Upstream recipes are extended, not copied ✔ Overrides use the colon syntax … CONFIGURATION ✖ Product configuration lives in layers, not local.conf [warning] local.conf:4: IMAGE_FSTYPES: product configuration belongs in your distro, machine or image why: local.conf is per developer and not versioned with the product. fix: Move image contents to your image recipe and policies to your distro. (https://docs.yoctoproject.org/what-i-wish-id-known.html) … $ echo $? 0 With --fail-on warning the same review exits 2. Option Effect --practices review the active profile (or --profile NAME) with the project's bitloom-practices.json --format text|md|json the report format -o FILE write the report to a file --fail-on error exit status 2 when an active rule at error fails (the default) --fail-on warning also fail on warnings --fail-on never always exit 0: report only

title: Practical limits
text: The review reads files; it does not run BitBake. Values computed at parse time are outside its view (see Variables above). Your layers are the layers inside the project folder that are not known upstream layers; a layer kept elsewhere is treated as upstream. Practices are in the web dashboard and on the command line, not in the TUI.

title: Teams, CI/CD and setup
text: Teams, CI/CD and setup Features for organisations with many products, images, devices and build machines. Bitloom still runs one build at a time per build service: a serial queue avoids concurrent BitBake servers fighting over a build directory.

title: Headless CI runs
text: bitloom --ci runs operations without the TUI, with the same profiles, runtimes, serial queue and history: bitloom --config ci/profiles.json --state .ci \ --ci kas-build --ci build:core-image-minimal \ --profile product-a --profile product-b \ --junit results.xml --summary summary.json --ci ACTION[:TARGET] is repeatable; bitloom --list-actions lists the identifiers. Interactive operations and operations needing other inputs are refused. --profile is repeatable: the matrix runs every operation on every profile, serially. --annotations auto|github|gitlab|plain (default auto, from GITHUB_ACTIONS/GITLAB_CI) folds each job's log into a collapsible section and turns failed tasks and the most frequent warnings into annotations. --junit writes one test case per job (failed tasks, last errors and task log paths in the failure); --summary writes JSON with status, exit code, duration, task and setscene counts, sstate hit rate, warning groups, failed tasks and the images produced. Operations the profile's Yocto release does not provide are skipped with a warning (<skipped> in JUnit), so one matrix can span Scarthgap and Wrynose. --fail-fast stops at the first failure. SIGTERM and Ctrl+C stop the running job cleanly. Exit code 0 means every job that ran succeeded. Example GitHub Actions step: - run: bitloom --config ci/profiles.json --state .ci --ci kas-build --junit results.xml --summary summary.json - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 if: always() with: { name: bitloom-reports, path: "res

title: Team profiles
text: Share profiles through NFS or a repository with include: { "active": "product-a", "include": ["/nfs/yocto/team-profiles.json", "../shared/profiles.json"], "profiles": [ { "name": "my-experiment", "root": "/home/me/src/product", "mode": "kas-container" } ] } Included files contain a profiles array. Relative paths resolve from the profiles file; environment variables such as $HOME expand. Team profiles are read-only: the profile editor shows only your own, the switcher (P) marks them team, and clone creates an editable copy. An unreachable include is reported in Configuration instead of preventing Bitloom from starting.

title: Setup and infrastructure checks
text: Configuration and bitloom --doctor (exit code 2 when a check warns) include host checks that new team members otherwise discover one failed build at a time: CPU cores, memory, Python, UTF-8 locale, inotify watches, open-files limit, Docker/Podman, kas and git, and on WSL a reminder to keep builds on the Linux filesystem. They also report the filesystem of the build directory, TMPDIR, DL_DIR and SSTATE_DIR. TMPDIR or the build directory on NFS, CIFS, 9p or drvfs is a warning (locking, hard links, speed); shared downloads and sstate on network storage are fine, with a reminder that a read-only SSTATE_MIRRORS plus a local SSTATE_DIR scales better when many builders write. Configuration → n (or bitloom --doctor --network) probes the shared infrastructure configured in local.conf: SSTATE_MIRRORS, PREMIRRORS, MIRRORS (TCP reachability or mounted file:// paths), BB_HASHSERVE, BB_HASHSERVE_UPSTREAM and PRSERV_HOST. It never downloads or authenticates.

title: Many images and machines
text: Artifacts → m shows the image matrix: for every MACHINE in tmp/deploy/images, each image file with its size and date and the package count from its manifest, plus SDK installers.

title: Many devices
text: Configure devices in Developer → Devices (SSH, labgrid places, console and test commands). Fleet status (Developer → Board view → Fleet status, or bitloom --fleet) probes every device at once with SSH BatchMode or labgrid-client show, with timeouts, and writes fleet-status.json. --fleet exits 1 unless every device is online, so a lab health job can gate on it.

title: Builds started elsewhere
text: BitBake writes the complete console of every build to tmp/log/cooker/<MACHINE>/<timestamp>.log. Builds → c lists them, classified from their task summary, including builds started from a terminal, a script or CI. Opening one gives the same search, errors-only filter and reports as a Bitloom job, without having had Bitloom running at the time. The web dashboard lists them under the history. Screenshot Console builds picker

title: Project launcher scripts
text: Many products wrap kas in a script that selects the configuration through an environment variable, for example YML=board.yml ./scripts/kas-wrapper.sh build. The wrapper runtime uses such a script: { "name": "board", "root": "/home/me/src/product", "mode": "wrapper", "launcher": ["./scripts/kas-wrapper.sh"], "launcher_shell": ["shell", "-c", "{command}"], "environment": { "YML": "boards/board.yml", "KAS_WORK_DIR": "/home/me/work/board" } } kas operations become launcher + subcommand: Build kas configuration runs ./scripts/kas-wrapper.sh build. Every other command runs through launcher_shell: bitbake -e busybox becomes ./scripts/kas-wrapper.sh shell -c 'bitbake -e busybox'. Profile environment variables (such as YML) reach the script; KAS_WORK_DIR/KAS_BUILD_DIR locate the build directory as for kas profiles. For the TUI to run BitBake commands, queries and runtime probes, the script must forward a shell command into the build environment (kas's shell -c, or whatever launcher_shell names) and keep standard input open (docker run -i) for Analysis and Developer probes. Health checks verify that the launcher exists and is executable.

title: Team chat notifications
text: Point the build service at a Slack, Teams or Mattermost incoming webhook (or an ntfy topic the team subscribes to) in Configuration → o: every long build on a shared build machine posts its outcome, profile, duration and failing task log, with no TUI attached. See Daily helpers.

title: Profiles from other versions
text: Profiles and history written by a newer or older Bitloom load with unknown keys ignored (Configuration lists them). The build service reports its version: when it is older than the client, the TUI and the web dashboard ask you to restart it when idle (bitloom --service-stop).

title: Developer workbench
text: Developer workbench Press F10 to open Developer, or reach it with F8/F9 or the sidebar. The workbench implements all fourteen workflows identified in the research roadmap, in sixteen views. It works through the selected host, kas, container or kas-container profile. Runtime paths are resolved inside that profile; they are not silently interpreted as host paths. For installation, building Bitloom and preparing a real Yocto workspace, start with the testbook. Its Developer acceptance cases cover every view and operation below. Sample demo mode does not provide BitBake. Screenshot Actual Developer workbench with evaluated recipe assignment history

title: Everyday controls
text: Select a view and enter the recipe in the top recipe field. Use mc:debug:busybox for a configured BitBake multiconfig. Clear the field for a global variable query. Read the placeholders in the two context fields. Their meaning changes with the view: variable name, runtime directory, report path, image or device. Choose Inspect. Queries acquire the same build-directory ownership as queued builds and run only while the queue is idle. Parsing metadata may take several seconds. Move through the table with arrows. Enter / Open opens the selected runtime file at its source line, navigates a directory, or displays signature evidence. Tab moves between controls. Logs/scripts are read-only; editable metadata receives backups and external-change checks. Select an operation and choose Run to queue a build, SDK or offline check, or open its existing command dialog. Inspect itself is an evidence query, not a build request. Operation buttons scroll horizontally in a narrow terminal. At 80×24 the table stacks above the report; at 60×20 it shrinks further. F10, F8/F9 and keyboard focus remain available. Ctrl+Q exits the interface; a running service build continues. F5 opens explicit interruption choices.

title: Capture, compare and refresh
text: Capture writes a private, timestamped JSON file under <state>/exports. The first capture fills the baseline field; later captures preserve it. Inspect after an edit or build, then choose Compare: it compares the current report to that baseline and saves a separate comparison export. Enter another capture path to change the baseline. Captures include the profile and original job reference where available; credential-like fields are redacted. The workbench checks recorded file fingerprints every fifteen seconds while visible and idle. An edit makes the report STALE; inspect again before capturing or comparing. External edits and runtime editor saves invalidate capability data too. Fingerprint and directory scans are bounded, so Inspect remains the authoritative explicit refresh.

title: Create a layer and recipe
text: Choose New layer. Enter a new absolute runtime directory, recipe name, layer collection, copyright owner and supported layer series. Select CMake, Meson, Make, Python or Rust. These are complete small source fixtures with an MIT license, matching LIC_FILES_CHKSUM, source files and layer.conf; use devtool add/recipetool for an existing external project. Preview shows every file and registration change. Fields returns to editing. Cancel creates nothing. Create + register refuses existing destinations, including symlinks. For host/direct-container profiles, registration is queued through bitbake-layers. For kas profiles, Bitloom writes a new host YAML overlay including the original configuration and local runtime layer, and selects a new derived profile; the original YAML/profile is preserved. Registration is complete when the installed release can parse the selected composition: check Show configured layers and Show recipe appends, then build the recipe. For the container experiment use /work/meta-bitloom-dev, recipe bitloom-hello, collection bitloomdev, series scarthgap, and a new kas-bitloom-dev.yml. The overlay adds the recipe to IMAGE_INSTALL. Build the recipe first, then core-image-minimal. Edit files/source/main.c through Runtime browser, change the greeting, rebuild and inspect the result. Choose different paths/names for a second experiment; the wizard does not overwrite an existing layer. Screenshot Actual layer wizard preview; no files created for this capture

title: Clone and compare configuration
text: Clone, also available in F4, copies a profile into a distinct absolute build directory. For kas it preserves KAS_WORK_DIR so local layers and source repositories remain available, and sets a separate absolute KAS_BUILD_DIR. kas-container mounts an external build directory as /build. Set optional machine/distro profile overrides, then select the clone. The YAML's resolved settings remain authoritative; inspect the actual kas dump before building. Changing machine/distro in a clone does not rewrite your original YAML. The queue remains serial; separate profiles do not enable concurrent BitBake invocations. Docker Snap may have a private daemon /tmp: a host directory can be empty while its container mount contains the complete build. Prepare new kas workspace repairs only the top directory of an empty, separately configured work mount. It refuses a nonempty directory owned by another user. Runtime paths remain /work/...; read/write them using Bitloom rather than guessing a host mapping.

title: IDE path mapping
text: For a host-accessible container checkout, add an explicit mapping in F4: "source_mappings": { "/work": "/home/you/yocto-work" } Export IDE mappings / database writes a private export with evaluated paths and, when available, a mapped compile_commands.json. Mapping respects directory boundaries and compiler path arguments. Configure the real host-visible path; mapping a Docker-private path does not copy files or create a working SDK. For daemon-private workspaces, use an IDE/container context with actual source/sysroot access. Generate IDE SDK probes release support before queueing devtool ide-sdk; supported build systems, SDK configuration and a matching target image are prerequisites for native IDE builds/debugging.

title: Offline and security checks
text: Prepare source mirrors runs fetchall with BB_GENERATE_MIRROR_TARBALLS in a temporary post-read configuration. Verify fetch offline runs BitBake fetchall with BB_NO_NETWORK; Verify full build offline applies BB_NO_NETWORK to the complete target build. Results, arguments and logs enter normal history. These checks cover BitBake fetchers; kas bootstrap may still need network for repositories/images. Fetch readiness and full-build readiness are separate outcomes. Restore deliberately broken URIs/checksums before verification. Run release-supported CVE/SPDX actions in F2, find the actual JSON report through Runtime browser, then inspect it in CVE / SBOM review. Existing issue statuses remain intact. Review exceptions are private local records with mandatory owner/reason/expiry; expired reviews are visibly labelled. Missing or unsupported reports do not produce an empty, apparently clean security result. An unpatched finding alone is not an exploitability assessment.

title: Boards and console
text: Choose Devices to edit <state>/devices.json. Example for a board you own: { "devices": [{ "name": "qemu-lab", "ssh": "root@192.0.2.10", "test_argv": ["ssh", "-o", "BatchMode=yes", "{device}", "bitloom-hello"], "console_argv": ["picocom", "-b", "115200", "/dev/ttyUSB0"] }] } Replace example addresses and serial paths with actual equipment. An optional labgrid_place enables labgrid show/acquire/release/power cycle/console using the installed labgrid-client and its environment. Test/console arrays are your explicit local commands; placeholders include {device}, {artifact}, {recipe} and {place}. Use a dedicated board and record ownership before changing it. Device status runs a real SSH or labgrid query. Tests and deploy require an exported local artifact whose SHA-256 is saved with device/job evidence. Devtool deploy transfers the recipe's workspace outputs; the referenced image hash is context, not proof that image was flashed. Your test_argv can invoke a real board-specific deployment/test tool if required. Serial sessions use the real terminal and util-linux script to retain a transcript and actual exit status; exits are controlled by the console program. Hardware is never simulated as successful.

title: Capabilities and stopping
text: Optional command-center task actions probe the selected recipe's actual listtasks, with a short-lived cache invalidated by profile/metadata changes. Missing testimage/ptest/kernel/security tasks are rejected before queueing with the observed prerequisite. Missing ide-sdk is also rejected. Configuration and report parsing remains release-dependent. For newly owned kas-container jobs, Runner gives each Docker/Podman container a unique Bitloom name/label. Force stop targets that exact container and records its stop result; confirmed termination of its namespace permits recovery for recipes observed active. Graceful draining remains available only where the actual BitBake client can receive the documented signal. An arbitrary kas wrapper or existing external container still requires server verification; wrapper exit alone is insufficient. Shutdown evidence separates observations from confirmation. Screenshot Actual buildstats and runtime resource evidence The validation report distinguishes real kas-container builds/probes, fixture parser tests and hardware/IDE/kernel experiments still requiring an operator. Reproduce evidence with python tools/validate_developer.py --build; add --image for a new full minimal-image build. The helper prepares a dedicated workspace, writes a generated test overlay/profile and preserves original integration configuration. It deliberately introduces and restores one failing task after successful offline checks.

title: Action-specific requirements
text: Clean recipe + sstate: Removes this recipe's local shared state. Avoid with shared caches in active use. Clean recipe + sstate + downloads: Removes recipe sources and local shared state. Generate SPDX SBOM: Requires create-spdx in your image configuration. Run image tests: Requires testimage configuration and suitable target runner. Build ptest packages: Recipe must inherit ptest and ptest must be enabled. Custom command (argument list): Parsed as argv. Shell operators are not interpreted. Save kernel defconfig: Writes a minimal defconfig of the current kernel configuration to the kernel's build folder (${B}/defconfig): copy it to your layer as a starting point. U-Boot menuconfig: Configures the machine's bootloader (PREFERRED_PROVIDER_virtual/bootloader, usually u-boot) in a terminal. Keep the result with U-Boot diffconfig. Export U-Boot config changes: Writes the changes made with menuconfig as a fragment.cfg in the bootloader's work folder: add it to SRC_URI in a u-boot append in your layer. Run recipe CVE check (cve-check): Requires the cve-check class and CVE database. Removed in 6.0 Wrynose: use sbom-cve-check. Recipe CVE analysis from its SBOM (sbom-cve-check): Analyses the recipe SBOM without building the software. The recipe must inherit sbom-cve-check-recipe; reports go to DEPLOY_DIR_IMAGE. Create recipe SBOM (SPDX 3): Recipe-level SBOM used by sbom-cve-check-recipe. Generate VEX metadata: Requires INHERIT += "vex". Produces per-recipe and image VEX reports in DEPLO

text: The static documentation was exercised in Chromium 153 using Playwright: capability filtering, runtime profile examples, screenshot dialog, all generated HTML manuals and a 390-pixel mobile viewport passed. No JavaScript page errors or failed resources were observed. The site and publishing workflow are committed. Local browser checks do not claim a public Pages deployment.

title: Screenshots and GIF
text: The real-kas-* images show the verified build and its actual environment/dependencies. Other media is explicitly sample data. Media in assets/ was captured from the actual Textual app with Pilot. The sample workspace and controlled failure are clearly labelled demo data. title: Coverage boundaries
text: A passing minimal image build does not validate every board, old release, devtool operation, existing-container lifecycle, shared-cache topology, external device or optional testing/security class. Podman command construction is tested; a Docker execution does not prove an end-to-end Podman build. Graceful stop uses documented BitBake client behavior and single-signal unit verification; interrupting the full validation build was not used as a shortcut. Reference behavior: BitBake knotty UI shutdown handling, kas container guide.

title: Additional Analysis validation
text: The Analysis panel was tested for metadata content search, report export and sstate mode switching. Parser checks cover package architecture changes, conflicting manifest versions, missing current-task counts, zero denominators and repeated warning messages. The existing real kas build supplied 35 manifest package/architecture entries, a 0% initial sstate hit rate and 20 warning occurrences. Comparing its unchanged manifest against itself yielded no differences; changed manifests were validated with explicit test fixtures. No additional cold Yocto build was required for these read-only features.

title: Persistent service and runtime evidence validation
text: The new workflows were exercised against the same pinned kas-container and existing real build on 2026-10-10 with tools/probe_workflows.py. Runtime preflight found writable configuration, 842.8 GiB available and more than 63 million free inodes. The snapshot recorded two Git repositories, two manifests, 4,798 package size records and eight non-symlink artifacts. These are bounded snapshot counts, not counts of packages installed in the minimal image. Image provenance evaluated core-image-minimal and identified /bin/sh as owned by package/recipe busybox, with the inclusion path packagegroup-core-boot → busybox. Reported BusyBox package file bytes were 699,723; those are pkgdata file sizes, not compressed image size. Two real jobs completed through the independent service after the submitting RPC connections closed: bitbake -S printdiff busybox and a warm bitbake core-image-minimal. Both exited 0. The warm build attempted 4,064 tasks, all already current and all succeeded; its summary reported Current 1,854 with Wanted 0. This validates an incremental container build, not a second cold build. The service was stopped only after its queue finished. The runtime binary exporter transferred the actual 18,012,484-byte rootfs archive and verified SHA-256 f96d0d5d60d2465caa4ca5ce6b8d60e92c454e1a2a1df1e27d1c236db0f7cfe1, matching the original artifact. title: Theme and identity validation
text: The expanded suite passed 50 tests after adding twelve palettes. The theme UI test switches through every palette, verifies distinct actual screen backgrounds, cancels back to the original theme, saves Paper and restores it in a new session. Status/log colors use semantic palette colors, including the light palette. tools/capture_themes.py records actual terminal views for all twelve palettes and assembles the documentation GIF; NO_COLOR is cleared for those captures. The woven B icon is an original SVG with 32-, 180- and 512-pixel PNG exports used by README, site headers and favicons.

title: Package and launch instructions validation
text: The documented python -m build --no-isolation produced the 0.1.0 wheel and source archive after satisfying the declared setuptools >=61 requirement. The wheel was installed into a fresh temporary virtual environment and imported from its site-packages while running outside the checkout; CLI help, the twelve palettes, actual TUI startup and a switch to Paper were verified. The source archive includes README, Pages/manual sources and assets, integration YAML and the profile preparation tool. tools/prepare_validation.py recreated the local kas profile from the recorded workspace without starting a build or deleting history. The documented TUI launch opened the actual local profile/history in a terminal and exited with Ctrl+Q; its idle service was then stopped. Build, launch, local test, fresh-machine setup, reconnect and documentation preview commands are covered in README and the user guide. These packaging checks do not claim another cold Yocto build.

title: Fresh demo setup and terminal resizing
text: setup-demo.sh --no-launch was run against a fresh temporary source copy without .venv, in a directory whose name contains spaces. It created the virtual environment, installed dependencies and generated demo metadata successfully. The installed app then launched at 80 × 24 and opened its command dialog using F2. Scrollbar tracks and corners now use each theme's surface palette, and log panes only show vertical scrollbars when needed. Theme tests check log and analysis backgrounds and scrollbar colors across all twelve palettes. The README and landing page open with an idle demo capture. Failure captures elsewhere show the explicitly labelled diagnostic sample; they do not represent a Bitloom failure or the real kas-container build result.

title: Release packaging

Local packaging generated versioned source archives, wheels, Debian packages and SHA256SUMS for 0.2.0 and 0.2.1; all checksum checks passed. Seven release tests verify stable version validation and synchronized distribution/runtime versions. The .deb was actually installed in a disposable kas container, where /usr/bin/bitloom --help succeeded and the runtime version was checked. No package was installed on the host. The final source, wheel and Debian package were also checked for the MIT license. This verifies local packaging; the GitHub release workflow has not been dispatched or published during this work.

Version 0.2.2 source, wheel and Debian assets were generated with the new names; the Debian package was installed in a disposable container, where the Bitloom CLI and runtime import/version succeeded. title: Bitloom manual testbook
text: Bitloom manual testbook This is an executable learning path and acceptance checklist, not a report of tests already performed. Run it yourself against your environment. All project text and evidence should remain in English. Record PASS, FAIL or N/A with the reason and a log/screenshot. Do not count an unavailable device, class or runtime as a successful test.

title: Contents
text: Guided tour — start here: every feature on the two built workspaces, no long builds Build and installation Launch with kas-container UI and profile acceptance Build, downloads and recipe tasks Create a layer and recipes from the TUI Editing and devtool Logs, reports and analysis State, reconnect and interruption Caches Runtime variants and optional features Every command-center action Record results and restore the experiment Developer acceptance Keyboard, web, compliance, Studio and teams New here? Follow chapter 0 first. For full acceptance, run chapters 1–5 first. Image builds, SDKs, security databases and hardware tests take substantially longer than UI/navigation tests. Chapter 11 is the command coverage ledger; it references fixtures and prerequisites from the preceding chapters.

title: 0. Guided tour — start here
text: One path through every feature of the TUI and the web dashboard, in an order where each step builds on the previous one. It uses the two real kas workspaces that are already built on this machine, so no step runs a long build: the longest optional step takes about nine minutes, everything else seconds. Build times below were measured on these workspaces with a warm sstate cache. Each step says what to do and what you should see. If you do not see it, note the step number: that is a bug.

title: Before you start (5 minutes)
text: Two terminals in the repository, both with the project environment: cd ~/…/yoctotui # the Bitloom checkout source .venv/bin/activate # fresh checkout: ./setup-demo.sh --dev --no-launch first export PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" # kas-container lives in the venv bitloom --state .validation --service-stop # only if a service from an older Bitloom is still running The profiles file .validation/profiles.json already contains the two built workspaces: Profile Release Work directory kas-scarthgap Scarthgap 5.0 LTS (poky) ~/bitloom-kas-validation kas-wrynose Wrynose 6.0 LTS (split repositories, sbom-cve-check enabled) ~/bitloom-kas-wrynose If the file is missing, recreate it without building: python tools/prepare_validation.py --release both --work ~/bitloom-kas-validation --wrynose-work ~/bitloom-kas-wrynose. Terminal A, the TUI: COLORTERM=truecolor bitloom --config .validation/profiles.json --state .validation Terminal B, the web dashboard (same service, same history): bitloom --web --config .validation/profiles.json --state .validation --port 9000 Open the printed http://127.0.0.1:9000/#token=… in a browser. Keep both side by side for the rest of the tour.

title: Stage 1 — Find your way around (no builds, 5 minutes)
text: # Do You should see 1.1 TUI: press ?, scroll, Esc. The keyboard reference: global keys, every section's letters, nano keys for editors. 1.2 Press 1 … 9, 0, then [ and ]. Each section opens; the rail marks it; the footer shows the section's own letters. 1.3 Press P, choose kas-scarthgap, then P again and kas-wrynose. The top bar shows scarthgap 5.0 LTS then wrynose 6.0 LTS within a second. 1.4 Web: press 1 … 6, then ?. The six views fade in; the help lists the web keys. 1.5 Web: Ctrl+K, type scarth, Enter; then Ctrl+K, wry, Enter. The palette switches profile; the release chip changes. 1.6 TUI: F7, try Linen and High Contrast, Esc. The palette previews live; Esc restores yours.

title: Stage 2 — Inspect the real workspace (no builds, 10 minutes, profile kas-wrynose)
text: # Do You should see 2.1 2 Recipes. Type busybox in the search, Enter on the recipe. About 1300 entries (layers, recipes, appends, classes, kas files only); the preview shows the recipe; Enter opens it read-only in the editor (^X closes). 2.2 t (tree), expand meta. Layers with their recipes; no BitBake test fixtures, no CI YAML. 2.3 3 Task logs, filter do_compile, open one. Thousands of task logs; the log opens with search (^W). 2.4 5 Caches, s (scan), then w (tmp/work). Downloads: about 1000 files and 14 GiB, .done markers hidden and counted. tmp/work: about 60 GiB per recipe, largest first, with rm_work advice (≈7 s). 2.5 6 Artifacts, then m, s, i. Image matrix per MACHINE; SBOM quality (SPDX 3.0.1, 37 installed packages, PURL/licence 100%); rootfs inventory of the newest image. 2.6 1 Builds, c (console builds). Every BitBake run of this build directory, also those started outside Bitloom, each marked success, failed or interrupted. Enter opens one in Builds. 2.7 Web: 2 Recipes, 3 Task logs, 4 Image, 5 SBOM & CRA. The same data in the browser; the SBOM gauges animate.

title: Stage 3 — First real jobs, followed in both interfaces (≈1 minute of builds)
text: # Do You should see 3.1 9, o (notifications): tick success and failed, set the minimum to 0, ^O. Saved; from now on every job end raises a desktop notification (a Windows notification on WSL). 3.2 TUI: t, type busybox, Enter. Build target · busybox queued and done in ≈10 s (nothing to rebuild); toast/notification Completed. The web history shows the same job at once. 3.3 F2, type force, choose Force compile, Enter (target busybox). ≈45 s: live output, task count N/M, active BitBake tasks, ETA once enough tasks ran; the web progress bar is striped and moving. 3.4 When it ends: 1, select it, d (compare). Comparison with the previous force compile, if any; otherwise with the closest earlier run. Run 3.3 again and press d: durations and task counts side by side. 3.5 e (errors only), / search busybox, x (export), i (summary). Filtered views of the same log; the export lands in .validation/exports. 3.6 Web: select the job, tabs Summary, Sstate reuse, Warnings, Timings, Compare (u o w m d). Toaster-style reports computed from the log.

title: Stage 4 — Failures and their diagnosis (≈10 seconds; optional real story ≈9 minutes)
text: # Do You should see 4.1 t, type no-such-recipe, Enter. Fails in ≈5 s; toast Build failed; the web raises the same failure toast. 4.2 7 Analysis, type Failure diagnosis, a. Category metadata, the root-cause lines (Nothing PROVIDES) and the next step. 4.3 t, type a; id, Enter. Refused before queueing: Not a BitBake target. 4.4 Optional, Wrynose with sbom-cve-check: after 3.3, build core-image-minimal (t, Enter). ≈4.5 min, then do_sbom_cve_check fails. f opens the failed task log; Analysis → Failure diagnosis says stale SBOM and gives the fix. 4.5 Optional fix: F2, Custom command, bitbake core-image-minimal -C create_image_sbom_spdx, Enter. ≈3.5 min, success. 6, v then shows the new CVE report.

title: Stage 5 — Stop, retry, detach (≈1 minute)
text: # Do You should see 5.1 Start the force compile again (3.3); while it runs press s. The stop dialog: Graceful stop is disabled with the reason (kas runtimes expose no BitBake client to signal); Let finish leaves it running. 5.2 Choose Force + recovery. The job's own container is stopped and the job ends cancelled; recovery offers bitbake -c clean busybox for the recipe that was running. Accept or skip it. 5.3 r (retry). The same command queued again with its original profile. 5.4 While it runs: Ctrl+Q, then launch the TUI again (terminal A command). The job kept running in the service; the TUI reconnects to it and its output. 5.5 Web: on a running job, hover Graceful, then press s. Graceful is disabled with the same reason; s asks for confirmation and stops the job.

title: Stage 6 — Developer workbench (≈2 minutes of probes in the container)
text: 8 Developer. Choose the view with v, set the field, press i (Inspect). Each probe runs inside the kas container. # View and input You should see 6.1 Variable history, recipe busybox, variable SUMMARY. ≈8 s: every assignment of SUMMARY with file and line (/work/openembedded-core/…). 6.2 Recipe context. ≈13 s: PN, PV, FILE, DL_DIR and the rest of the evaluated recipe. 6.3 Runtime capabilities. ≈25 s: bitbake, devtool, runqemu… found or unavailable in the container. 6.4 Image regressions, field blank. ≈20 s: the build target's installed packages and sizes from buildhistory. c captures a baseline; after a rebuild d compares. 6.5 Build performance. The slowest tasks of the latest real build (sbom-cve-check database fetches first). 6.6 Kernel fragments with the field blank. A clear message asking for a .cfg path (no traceback). 6.7 Runtime browser, Enter on build, then on a file. Directory listing inside the container; files open in the runtime editor.

title: Stage 7 — Studio: your own layer and recipe (≈1 minute of build)
text: # Do You should see 7.1 2, c (Studio), choose Application recipe. Layer new layer… meta-tour, name tour-hello, build system make. The preview lists every file: layer.conf, licence, Makefile, tour-hello_1.0.bb. 7.2 ^O (create, use for this profile). Files written; kas-studio-meta-tour.yml appended to the profile's kas files; target set to tour-hello. 7.3 b. ≈45 s on Wrynose (≈75 s on Scarthgap): the recipe builds; the new layer appears in Recipes. 7.4 Web: 6 Studio, Distribution. Live preview of conf/distro/acme.conf; nothing is written until Create files. 7.5 Clean up when done: F4, remove :kas-studio-meta-tour.yml from kas_file, ^O; delete meta-tour/ and the overlay. The profile builds the plain image again.

title: Stage 8 — SBOM, CVE and CRA (no builds)
text: # Do You should see 8.1 6, v. ≈1800 unpatched of ≈21500 assessed, critical first; detail with CVSS vector and link. 8.2 / type openssl; r on a row: owner, reason, expiry ^O. Filtered list; the review appears in the Review column. 8.3 x, choose Markdown report; repeat with HTML, SARIF. Files in .validation/exports: the Markdown links every CVE to NVD, CVE.org and OSV; open the HTML in a browser and print it to PDF. 8.4 9, c (CRA readiness). Every check from real evidence; Unpatched vulnerabilities warns; dispositions now count your review. 8.5 9, s (SBOM settings). Move through the options; Esc (do not apply). Each option explains itself; Generate SPDX SBOMs shows on (default) on Wrynose; on kas-scarthgap the Wrynose-only options show n/a. 8.6 P → kas-scarthgap, F2, type sbom-cve. (not in this release) with the Scarthgap alternative (cve-check). 8.7 Web: 5, Export menu → Markdown report. The same report downloads.

title: Stage 8b — The image, file by file, and what each release can do (no builds)
text: # Do You should see 8b.1 Web on kas-wrynose: 4 (Image). core-image-minimal · qemux86-64 from its tar.bz2: ≈29 MiB on the device, ≈370 files, ≈34 packages; biggest package the kernel image (≈13 MiB), then libcrypto3 · openssl, libc6 · glibc; biggest folders /boot, /usr, /lib. 8b.2 Open etc, select motd. base-files 3.0.14, layer meta · upstream, in core-image-minimal (pulled in by packagegroup-core-boot), the existing appends in meta-poky and meta-selftest, the text of the file, and the advice to add a base-files_%.bbappend to your layer. 8b.3 Change it with an append. Esc at the end without creating. Studio opens a Recipe append already filled in: base-files, recipes-core, file motd; the planned files/motd holds the current device text (toast Starting from the device's file). 8b.4 Type libc6 in Which recipe installs…, Enter; then select /etc/passwd. libc6 is the renamed glibc package, pulled in by busybox, eudev, kmod…; /etc/passwd is in no package, with the explanation (useradd, EXTRA_USERS_PARAMS). 8b.4b Image: Services. Select syslog. Then bitloom --config .validation/profiles.json --state .validation --services. sysvinit · 20 started at boot; init scripts in boot order (banner.sh S02, sysfs.sh S02, mountall.sh S03, udev S04…), then shutdown (halt, reboot) and helpers; udev rules from eudev with 80-net-name-slot.rules disabled in /etc. syslog opens /etc/init.d/syslog (owner root, busybox-syslog · busybox). The CLI prints the same list. 8b.4c Demo (bitloom --web --demo), pro

title: Stage 8c — Best practices (no builds)
text: # Do You should see 8c.1 Web on kas-wrynose: 7 (Practices). A score around 80 %, Needs attention grouped by area; LAYERSERIES_COMPAT includes the release you build fails on meta-acme/conf/layer.conf (scarthgap, the project builds wrynose) if the Studio test layer is still there; upstream layers are not judged. 8c.2 All rules: switch off Each layer has a SECURITY.md, set rm_work keeps tmp/work small to error.
